question: to the Commission Yvan Verougstraete (Renew) Subject:

According to several sources, a US platform called ‘freedom.gov’ is being developed with the stated aim of offering EU citizens a free VPN service that would enable them to circumvent the application of EU legislation, notably the Digital Services Act and the Digital Markets Act. Touted as a ‘freedom of expression’ initiative, the project would in fact make it possible to access, from EU territory, content that is regulated or banned under EU law, including hate speech and manipulative or illegal content. 1.

Does the Commission consider that a project backed by stakeholders with close ties to a foreign administration and expressly designed to neutralise the effect of EU law constitutes an attack on Europe’s regulatory sovereignty?
Does it consider that such an initiative could constitute a form of digital interference by a third country?
What specific steps will it take to ensure that EU law is implemented effectively and to prevent any organised attempt to systematically circumvent it?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.4.2026) The Commission has no specific comment to make on potential plans of the freedom.gov initiative and does not speculate on design or intent. The Commission does not block websites in the EU. Only Member States' authorities may block a website if it is illegal under national or European law. This includes websites promoting child-sexual abuse material, terrorist content or copyright-infringing material. The Commission has a responsibility to enforce its laws, including the Digital Services Act1, effectively, fairly and without discrimination towards all companies operating in the EU.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single
Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj/eng.
